Sources & workbook map

What came from Excel, what changed, and what still needs review.

Fluid planner

Workbook origin: Fluids!C3:H20. Canine maintenance = 132 × kg0.75; feline = 80 × kg0.75, both in mL/day. Deficit = kg × dehydration fraction × 1,000 mL.

Primary clinical reference: 2024 AAHA Fluid Therapy Guidelines, Section 3, Box 3 and Table 9. These equations are among the listed options. The guideline calls for individualized plans, replacement generally over 12–24 hours, and reassessment.

Owner-approved changes: replacement hours apply only to the deficit. Both species use hourly ongoing losses. Initial-estimate mode credits selected boluses against the original deficit; reassessed-estimate mode does not subtract them again. This choice of workflow is an application design decision, not a verbatim AAHA instruction.

Scope: adult canine/feline calculation. No pediatric multiplier, resuscitation protocol, fluid selection, or automatic adjustment for concurrent enteral water, medications, nutrition, renal disease, or cardiac disease. Account for those when prescribing.

Potassium supplementation

Workbook origin: Fluids!L3:V12. Original equation: KCl mL = selected mEq/kg/hr × kg × (bag mL ÷ fluid mL/hr) ÷ stock mEq/mL. Stock concentration is fixed at 2 mEq/mL in Excel. The website defaults to 2 mEq/mL, locked until explicitly unlocked.

Primary clinical reference: 2024 AAHA Fluid Therapy Guidelines, Section 5, hypokalemia discussion and Table 11. Workbook dose bands match the table. Mix KCl thoroughly, avoid boluses, and use controlled infusion equipment. Persistent hypokalemia warrants assessment of magnesium.

Application choices: clinician-selected supplemental target; all chart rows calculate live, and clicking a rate reveals the worked math. No automatic serum-K interpretation. Carrier potassium is excluded at the owner’s request. A separate input credits supplemental K from other infusions. An adjustable stock concentration and two preparation modes replace the original single-volume approximation. Arithmetic is derived from concentration × volume and rate × time; AAHA does not provide these exact application formulas.

Limits: no target above 0.5 mEq/kg/hr; no osmolarity, catheter, compatibility, monitoring-schedule, or renal-function assessment. Multi-additive mixtures in the same bag are not supported. Numerical checks do not constitute independent clinical validation.

Magnesium

Workbook origin: Fluids!L13:U20. The 1 and 0.5 mEq/kg/day options, 4 mEq/mL default, and total-Mg guide of 1.5–2.5 mg/dL come from the workbook. The guide is explicitly replaceable with the reporting laboratory’s interval; it is not asserted as a universal canine/feline range. Entered results locate a workbook row without automatically choosing a dose. The page labels these as workbook options; the normal-Mg/refractory-K option is not independently established here as a universal indication.

Primary case report: Smith, Hendricks & Centola, 2022, DOI 10.2147/VMRR.S358682 describes 1 mEq/kg/day IV CRI in one cat with severe hypomagnesemia. This is case-level evidence, not validation of every workbook option.

Formulation source: Hospira magnesium sulfate label lists 4.06 mEq/mL for its 50% product and requires dilution before IV use. The label is used for formulation information, not human dosing. Verify the actual vial; the workbook default remains 4 pending deliberate edit.

Timing clarification: amount = dose per day × kg × preparation hours/24. A 12-hour preparation contains half the daily amount. Final diluted volume is explicit; the tool does not select a clinically appropriate dilution, monitor renal function, or assess compatibility.

Phosphate / KPhos

Workbook origin: Fluids!L24:T35. Dose bands match Igor Yankin’s VetEmCrit phosphate reference (2024), an author’s clinical guidance rather than a consensus guideline. It describes 3 mmol phosphate/mL and 4.4 mEq K/mL for the US product, calcium incompatibility, and the need to account for accompanying potassium.

Changes: all K calculations reference the editable K concentration. One input set replaces the duplicated sheet inputs. Final-volume and existing-carrier-volume methods are explicit. A prominent selected-dose panel shows K from KPhos per kg per hour, per hour, and per preparation. Combined entered supplemental K is capped at 0.5 mEq/kg/hr as a tool constraint. Carrier K remains excluded per owner preference; the separate-infusion field accounts for other supplemental K.

Monitoring context: the author suggests phosphorus rechecks every 24 hours for the mild band, 12–24 hours for moderate, and 6–12 hours for severe; individualize to the patient. Renal function, calcium, compatibility, and the clinical indication require assessment. The tool does not calculate KCl co-mixing into the same bag.

Sodium workflow and workup additions

The high/low workflow grouping is an application synthesis, not a validated diagnostic rule. Heinz & Cook, Evaluation and Management of the Hyponatremic Patient (2022) supports the assessment framework and the sodium-plus-potassium response estimate. The per-liter estimate is scaled to the entered volume, which is approximate and cannot account for changing renal water handling or ongoing losses.

2024 AAHA, Section 5 supplies correction-limit, urgent-treatment, and base-fluid references. LRS, Plasma-Lyte, and 0.9% NaCl use sodium concentrations of 130, 140, and 154 mEq/L. Stock presets reflect the cited table’s formulations; verify the actual vial.

2023 AAHA canine hypoadrenocorticism testing guidance supports the resting-cortisol and ACTH-testing reference. This diagnostic branch applies to dogs and assumes no assay-interfering glucocorticoid exposure.

The glucose-correction tool retains the newer 2024 canine study’s 1.6 factor and the workbook equation; the older 2022 review’s alternative high-glucose adjustment is not substituted.

Sodium

Workbook origin: free water C24:I30; fluid mixing C31:I45 and C47:E60; glucose correction F47:I54.

Primary guideline: 2024 AAHA, Section 5, Tables 12A and 13A. Free-water calculations retain the 0.6 body-water fraction. Context-specific time estimates and a custom duration are explicit. Chronic correction is limited to 0.5 mEq/L/hr; measured response still requires serial monitoring.

Mixing changes: final volume means carrier replacement, not adding stock on top of an unchanged bag. Unreachable targets are rejected. The quick-math sodium outputs are calculated instead of copied from hardcoded cells. These are concentration-conservation equations, not patient-response models.

Primary correction-factor study: JAVMA 2024: sodium correction factor in dogs undergoing treatment for hyperglycemic crisis. Supports 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL glucose increment. The workbook equation uses glucose minus 100; feline application is labeled extrapolation. No correction is provided for glucose below 100 mg/dL.

Dextrose

Workbook origin: Fluids!L38:S41. Final-volume dilution math agrees with 2024 AAHA, Section 5, Table 14. Carrier replacement maintains the stated final volume. Editable stock and baseline dextrose concentrations replace the fixed 50%/0% assumptions. This is a mixing calculator, not a bolus protocol.

Blood collection and printable cage sheet

Workbook origin: Fluids!L44:U54. Defaults retain 60 mL/kg blood volume, an optional 15% reduction for the workbook’s sick/geriatric/obese group, 1% per 24 hours, and 10% per 14 days. These are labeled as workbook planning assumptions, not universal patient-specific safe limits. Clinician-approved collection volumes are separate optional fields.

NC3Rs blood-sampling principles discuss frequent-sampling fractions, minimizing blood removal, and lower estimates in older/obese animals. Their research-animal guidance is not a validation of the workbook’s entire ill-patient algorithm; their intervals also differ for larger repeat collections.

University of Kentucky laboratory-animal guidance emphasizes species variation and healthy-adult assumptions. These values are not substituted for the workbook model.

Lynch et al., hospital-acquired anemia in critically ill dogs and cats provides clinical context for tracking phlebotomy, not validation of the calculator thresholds. Record all removed blood, including discard, and incorporate other sheets when reviewing time-window totals.

Original workbook links

  • Fluids!M12 links to VetEmCrit IV potassium calculator. Accessible on review. Its serum-K bands differ from the workbook/AAHA table, so they were not substituted.
  • Fluids!H22 links to Vetcalculators fluid therapy page. Automated access returned HTTP 403; its content was not used for validation.

These are original workbook links, not evidence that every adjacent calculation originated there. Review date: October 17, 2026. Uploaded workbook remains unchanged.

Drugs: data model & review record

Drug entities hold stock concentration and category memberships; administration-specific preparation math is separate. Groups are filters, not combination protocols. Patient data stays in this page's memory.

Metoclopramide: workbook stock 5 mg/mL; CRI 1 and 2 mg/kg/day. SQ reference 0.2–0.5 mg/kg per dose from Merck Veterinary Manual. ANSES product information supports clinical precautions, not IV admixture compatibility. References checked October 17, 2026.

Review queue: workbook metoclopramide loading dose 0.05 mg/kg; dexmedetomidine total-unit label; propofol premedicated lower-volume formula uses 5 while dose cell says 2; local anesthetic maxima lack species; enrofloxacin 10 mg/kg lacks species restrictions; NSAID species and schedules need review; norepinephrine stock/rate labels need confirmation. These inconsistencies are not silently adopted as approved protocols.

The other drug references are workbook transcriptions. Assumed doses are prefilled at the single workbook dose or low end of its range; route/context variants have separate rows. These remain review-pending workbook profiles, not patient-specific prescriptions. No repeat interval, tablet rounding, or combination sedation protocol is generated. Norepinephrine calculates a pump rate from an explicitly prescribed rate and known prepared concentration only. Antibiotic indication and duration, Firstline integration, and anesthesia equipment references remain future work.

Rough GI-loss estimate

Craig B. Webb, Hepatic lipidosis: Clinical review drawn from collective effort, J Feline Med Surg. 2018;20:217–227, doi:10.1177/1098612X18758591. The initial fluid stabilization box gives 3–4 mL/kg per vomiting or diarrhea episode. This is a feline clinical rule of thumb, not a validated universal episode volume. Applying it to dogs is extrapolation. Default 3 mL/kg/episode was selected by the site owner; users may edit it.

Fluid Therapy in Hospitalized Patients, Part 1 recommends reassessing estimated ongoing losses in 4–6 hours. Reassess sooner when clinically indicated. AAHA 2024, Section 3 recommends incorporating ongoing input/output assessments into the fluid plan; it does not establish this episode multiplier.

Formula: kg × episodes × mL/kg/episode ÷ hours = additional mL/hr. Enter the interval represented by the episodes for an average ongoing rate. Count only losses still requiring replacement; do not duplicate losses already accounted for in the dehydration deficit. This helper replaces the ongoing-loss input when explicitly applied; it does not add itself to an existing loss estimate. It is not a urine-output, hemorrhage, resuscitation, or fluid-tolerance calculator. Measured volumes and patient response take precedence.

CRI concentration review

Norepinephrine concentrations and access cutoffs are workbook profiles, not validated veterinary maximums. No universal veterinary maximum was substantiated in the reviewed veterinary sources. Veterinary concentration references.

CRI workbook map & review

Order: Fentanyl, Lidocaine, Ketamine, Norepinephrine, Insulin, Reglan. Source workbook: Sx CRI, Fentanyl CRI, Fluids L57:U59, Sepsis D28:N104, DKA B32:K44, Drugs B33:J42. Unasyn, dopamine and electrolyte infusions excluded by owner.

All CRI calculators share the banner patient weight. Stock settings are locked by default. Prepared concentrations and selected doses remain explicit. Recipes solve stock volume + compatible diluent = stated final volume; manufacturer bag overfill is not estimated. Do not treat numeric tables as universal prescribing ranges.

Fentanyl: workbook 50/25/12.5 mcg/mL and patient-specific concentration = weight kg in mcg/mL, so 1 mL/hr corresponds to 1 mcg/kg/hr. Merck emergency opioid table distinguishes canine and feline dosing; workbook rows 1–10 are not a universal feline range.

Lidocaine: workbook 20/10 mg/mL, 20–70 mcg/kg/min comparison. MSD analgesic reference lists canine analgesic CRI 20–50 mcg/kg/min and cautions feline sensitivity. Upper workbook rows are retained for review, not endorsed as routine analgesic dosing. Feline calculations are disabled per owner. Ketamine: workbook 10/5/1 mg/mL and 0.1–0.6 mg/kg/hr; clinical references vary with context.

Norepinephrine: workbook stock 1 mg/mL (1000 mcg/mL), prepared 64/32/16/8 mcg/mL. Workbook peripheral/central limits 16/64 mcg/mL are retained as this site's profiles, not universal limits for every institution. Original rounded recipes did not always reach the printed concentration: these calculators instead solve an exact final volume (e.g., 8 mcg/mL × 60 mL requires 0.48 mL of 1000 mcg/mL stock + 59.52 mL diluent). Workbook mg/mcg text error corrected. Merck Rule of 20 supports mcg/kg/min units. Starting text 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min confirmed by owner. Monitor blood pressure/perfusion and catheter site; review fluid status before vasopressor use.

Insulin: the original workbook hourly profiles were canine 0.09 U/kg/hr, feline 0.045 U/kg/hr and euglycemic DKA 0.06 U/kg/hr. The site now defaults both dogs and cats to 0.1 U/kg/hr under the owner-selected fixed-rate DKA approach; see the evidence below. Feline 0.045 and workbook EDKA 0.06 remain explicit alternatives, not the automatic defaults. Regular U-100 insulin assumed explicitly; no glargine substitution. Volume and rate determine units needed, stock mL and nominal duration. Line priming/discard and adsorption require a validated local preparation protocol. Rudloff, Diabetic ketoacidosis in the cat (2017) discusses regular insulin infusions and line adsorption.

AAHA 2026 canine DKA and AAHA 2026 feline DKA are linked for clinical management; they do not validate every workbook profile. Glucose, ketones, electrolyte correction and patient status drive treatment. No BG/dextrose ladder or ketone stop threshold was automatically imported.

Reglan: workbook 2 mg/kg/day syringe and 1–2 mg/kg/day bag options; duration scales the daily amount for 6/12-hour syringes. Original undiluted hourly-equivalent calculation is shown separately as arithmetic, not an administration recommendation. See the Drugs source entry for dose and precaution references. Clinical and real-browser validation remain pending.

Insulin fixed-rate DKA default

Owner-selected default for dogs and cats: regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr IV CRI, editable. This is a protocol choice, not proof of superiority over a lower feline dose. No automatic euglycemic-DKA management is generated.

Gant, Barfield & Florey. Comparison of insulin infusion protocols for management of canine and feline diabetic ketoacidosis. JVECC 2024;34:23–30. doi:10.1111/vec.13354. Randomized trial: 20 dogs and 16 cats. Fixed-rate methods used 50 IU/500 mL at 1 mL/kg/hr = 0.1 IU/kg/hr. Dextrose was adjusted to support glucose while insulin treated ketosis. Fixed-rate treatment did not significantly hasten ketosis resolution; feline comparisons were limited. The abstract's 0.01 IU/kg/hr conflicts with the methods and results table, which indicate 0.1; this discrepancy is explicitly flagged.

Anderson, Rondeau & Hess. JVIM 2019;33:1593–1601. doi:10.1111/jvim.15518. Twelve cats received lispro or regular insulin initially at 0.09 U/kg/hr. The study compares insulin products, not higher versus lower starting doses.

Claus et al. JVECC 2010;20:509–517. doi:10.1111/j.1476-4431.2010.00567.x. Retrospective feline dose comparison did not demonstrate increased adverse sequelae with higher prescribed doses, but actual delivered doses were much lower because of variable-rate adjustments; it does not prove the safety or superiority of uninterrupted higher dosing.

Rudloff. JFMS 2017;19:1167–1174. Traditional feline regular-insulin mixture 1.1 U/kg in 250 mL at 10 mL/hr delivers 0.044 U/kg/hr, commonly rounded to 0.045, with subsequent glucose-based adjustments. This remains a labeled alternative. Follow a complete protocol for glucose, dextrose, potassium/phosphorus, ketones, line priming and patient reassessment. Reviewed October 17, 2026.

Insulin / dextrose charts: adaptation record

Primary quick reference selected by owner: >270 mg/dL None (ASK DVM); 200–270 2.50%; 127–200 5.00%; <127 consider increase to 7.5%/10%. This exact table is clinician-selected, not a verbatim published protocol. The shared 200 boundary is preserved with clinician selection noted. The prior combined fixed-rate reference is retained under More info / Other charts.

The owner selected a combined reference: Gant fixed-rate BG framework, with the workbook’s 2.5% tip and <100 mg/dL higher-concentration/feeding considerations. This exact combined chart is a clinical adaptation, not a prospectively validated protocol. Gant’s methods use 0.1 U/kg/hr, 5% dextrose below 270 mg/dL, target 180–270, and temporary insulin cessation below 126. Below-target escalation text is clinician-directed guidance, not a study-validated percentage ladder.

Original workbook DKA H37:K43: >300 None (ASK DVM); 250–299 2.5%; 150–249 2.5% plus feeding/NG note; 100–149 5%; <100 consider 7.5%/10% plus central-access/DVM and enteral support notes. The owner previously amended the workbook’s top boundary to ≥300; the current main fixed-rate chart instead uses 270 as its referenced threshold. The 2.5% bands are now retained as a separately labeled workbook tip.

NG nutrition or prescribed enteral carbohydrate is an adjunct, not a verified replacement for IV glucose rescue. A temporary insulin reduction/hold remains an explicit option; severe/symptomatic hypoglycemia requires immediate treatment and reassessment. No automated treatment changes are generated. Full clickable sources are provided at the bottom of the Insulin CRI page.

Chocolate toxicity

Calculator source record: Merck Veterinary Manual, Chocolate Toxicosis in Animals, February 2026. Canine methylxanthine exposure estimates; oz/grams, listed types, cocoa-% approximation and summed products. The calculator uses Merck references only. Numeric reference bands do not establish safety or predict death.

Local-anesthetic limits · approval status

The existing workbook displays local/regional lidocaine 2–4 mg/kg and bupivacaine 1–2 mg/kg. These are reference ranges, not approved species-specific maximum doses. The interface warns outside those ranges without imposing new limits. No safe combined-exposure ceiling is calculated.

Species, route, formulation, previous doses and their timing require clinician review. The existing feline lidocaine CRI prohibition remains specific to CRI and is not applied to local/regional use.

Further source review is required before enabling new limits: 2020 AAHA Anesthesia and Monitoring Guidelines for Dogs and Cats and Merck Veterinary Manual · Local and Regional Analgesic Techniques in Animals. Access to these external sources was blocked in this development environment; new numeric limits have not been verified or activated.
